# 2 Samuel Chapter 13 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 182r–183r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_013_page_001.jpg, 2SA_013_page_002.jpg, 2SA_013_page_003.jpg

---

**1** Some time later, trouble came from within David's own house. Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister named Tamar — and Amnon, David's firstborn, was consumed with desire for her. **2** Amnon was so obsessed with his sister Tamar that it made him physically sick. She was a virgin, closely guarded, and he saw no way to get to her. **3** But Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a very clever man. **4** He said, "What's wrong with you, prince? Day after day you look worse. Tell me what it is." Amnon said, "I'm in love with Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."

**5** Jonadab said, "Here's what you do. Go to bed and act sick. When your father comes to check on you, say, 'Please let my sister Tamar come and prepare some food for me. Let her make it where I can watch, and feed me with her own hand.'"

**6** So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. When the king came to see him, Amnon said, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of special cakes right here where I can see, so I can eat from her hand." **7** David sent word to Tamar at the palace: "Go to your brother Amnon's house and make some food for him."

**8** Tamar went to Amnon's house, where he was lying in bed. She took dough, kneaded it, shaped the cakes while he watched, and baked them. **9** Then she took the pan and served them to him, but he refused to eat. "Get everyone out of here!" Amnon ordered. Everyone left.

**10** Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the bedroom so I can eat from your hand." Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother in the inner room. **11** But when she brought them close for him to eat, he grabbed her and said, "Come to bed with me, sister."

**12** "No, my brother!" she cried. "Don't violate me! This is not how things are done in Israel. Don't commit this outrage! **13** Think of me — where would I go with my shame? And think of yourself — you would be treated as the lowest fool in Israel! Please, just speak to the king. He won't refuse you."

**14** But he would not listen. He was stronger than she was, and he overpowered her and raped her.

**15** Then suddenly, Amnon was filled with intense hatred for her. The hatred he felt was even stronger than the desire he had felt before. "Get up!" he said. "Get out!" **16** "No!" she said. "Throwing me out like this is an even greater wrong than what you've already done to me!" But he refused to listen.

**17** He called his personal servant. "Get this woman out of here," he said. "Put her out and bolt the door behind her."

**18** She was wearing the long-sleeved robe that the king's virgin daughters wore. His servant threw her out and barred the door.

**19** Tamar put ashes on her head. She tore the beautiful robe she was wearing. She placed her hand on her head and walked away wailing as she went.

**20** Her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon been with you?" He saw the answer on her face. "Be quiet for now, sister. He's your brother. Don't let this destroy you." And Tamar lived in Absalom's house, a desolate woman.

**21** When King David heard what had happened, he was furious. But he did nothing.

**22** Absalom never said a word to Amnon — not hostile, not friendly. Nothing. He simply hated him for what he had done to his sister Tamar.

**23** Two full years passed. Absalom had arranged a sheep-shearing festival at Baal-hazor near Ephraim, and he invited all the king's sons. **24** He went to the king personally. "Your servant is having a shearing," he said. "Would the king and his officials honor me by attending?" **25** "No, my son," the king replied. "If we all go, we'll be too much of a burden for you." Absalom pressed him, but David wouldn't go — though he gave him his blessing.

**26** "Well then," Absalom said, "at least let my brother Amnon come with us." The king said, "Why should he go with you?" **27** But Absalom kept pressing until David sent Amnon and all the king's sons.

**28** Absalom had already given his servants their orders: "Watch Amnon. When the wine has made him relaxed and cheerful, and I give you the signal — strike him down. Kill him. Don't be afraid — I'm the one giving the command. Be strong. Be brave."

**29** Absalom's men did exactly as he ordered. The other princes leapt to their feet, jumped on their mules, and fled.

**30** While they were still on the road, a report reached David: "Absalom has killed all the king's sons! Not one of them survived!" **31** The king stood up, ripped his robes apart, and threw himself on the ground. All his officials stood around him with their clothes torn.

**32** But Jonadab — David's nephew, the clever one — spoke up: "My lord must not think that all the young princes are dead. Only Amnon is dead. Absalom has been planning this from the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar. **33** So my lord the king should not grieve as though all his sons are dead. Only Amnon has died."

**34** Meanwhile, Absalom had fled. The lookout on watch raised his eyes and saw a large group of people coming down the road from the hillside. **35** Jonadab said to the king, "Look — the king's sons are coming! It's just as I said."

**36** He had barely finished speaking when the king's sons burst in, weeping loudly. The king and all his officials broke down and wept bitterly with them.

**37** Absalom fled to his grandfather Talmai son of Ammihud, the king of Geshur. And David grieved for his son every day.

**38** After fleeing to Geshur, Absalom stayed there for three years. **39** And the heart of King David ached to go to Absalom, for his grief over Amnon's death had finally run its course.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 2 — "obsessed... physically sick":** The Hebrew piles up the language of constriction and illness: *vayetser* (it was narrow/pressed for him) and *lehitchalot* (to make oneself sick). This is not love — it is obsession that manifests as physical deterioration. Amnon's desire is portrayed as a kind of disease from the very beginning, prefiguring the violence it will produce.

**Verse 6 — "special cakes":** The Hebrew *levivot* derives from *lev* (heart). These are heart-shaped cakes — an almost cruelly ironic detail. Amnon asks for food shaped like hearts while planning an act of heartless cruelty. The verb used for Tamar's preparation (*vattelabbev*) intensifies the wordplay.

**Verse 12 — "this outrage":** Tamar's speech is extraordinary. In the moments before her rape, she delivers a carefully reasoned legal and moral argument. She names the act (*te'anneniy* — the technical term for sexual violation), identifies it as a violation of Israelite social order (*nevalah*), and even proposes a legitimate solution (marriage with royal permission). She is more articulate and more rational than anyone else in this narrative.

**Verse 15 — the great reversal:** The narrator delivers one of the most devastating psychological observations in all of Scripture. The desire was never love — it was possession. Once Amnon possessed Tamar, the desire inverted into its mirror image: hatred. The Hebrew construction is carefully symmetrical, as if the narrator wants us to see that the love and the hatred were always the same force.

**Verse 18 — the torn robe:** The *ketonet passim* — the same phrase used for Joseph's famous coat in Genesis 37. The narrator is drawing a direct line between two acts of sibling violence. Joseph's brothers stripped him and threw him into a pit; Amnon strips Tamar of her dignity and throws her out. In both cases, the special garment — a symbol of the father's favor — becomes evidence of the crime.

**Verse 19 — Tamar's public mourning:** Tamar does three things: ashes on her head (mourning), tearing the robe (destroyed status), hand on her head (a gesture of grief or devastation). She does not hide what happened. Her wailing cry (*za'aqah*) is the same word used for Israel's cry under Egyptian oppression. She is making her violation public, even if no one will act on it.

**Verse 20 — Absalom's chilling restraint:** "Has Amnon your brother been with you?" — Absalom already knows. His instruction to "be silent" has been read as either protective or silencing. His words "don't take this to heart" are devastatingly inadequate as comfort — but they reveal that Absalom is already thinking, already planning. The narrator confirms: Absalom said nothing to Amnon, good or bad. He waited two years.

**Verse 21 — David's failure:** The MT says only that David was angry. The ancient Greek translation adds the crucial detail: "but he would not punish Amnon his son, because he loved him, for he was his firstborn." This omission in the Hebrew text may be accidental — but whether stated or unstated, David's inaction is the hinge on which the entire Absalom rebellion turns.

*— PNEUMA*
